title: Split one enormous commit into three
summary: A commit three back does four unrelated things. Stop the rebase on it, unwind it into the working tree, and commit the pieces separately.
mental_model: `edit` in a rebase todo means: apply this commit, then stop and hand me the shell. `git reset HEAD^` at that point removes the commit but leaves its changes in your working tree — now you can commit them in as many pieces as you like before continuing.

steps.title: Find the commit that does too much
steps.why: Three unrelated modules in one commit. It cannot be reverted selectively, cannot be cherry-picked to a release branch, and `git bisect` can only tell you 'one of these three things broke it'. Before any rewrite, drop a branch on the current tip — it costs nothing and gives you a name to compare against afterwards.
steps.expect: Three files in a single commit, and a backup branch on the tip.

steps.title: Stop the rebase on that commit
steps.why: Marking it `edit` tells rebase to apply it and then pause. The todo editor is scripted here to change the first line from pick to edit — exactly what you would type in the editor.
steps.expect: Stopped at the first commit, on a detached HEAD, with a clean tree.

steps.title: Unwind the commit without losing the work
steps.why: `reset HEAD^` moves back one commit and leaves the changes unstaged in the working tree. Nothing is deleted — the commit is dissolved into raw edits you can now re-commit however you like.
steps.expect: The three files are back as untracked changes, and the commit is gone.

verify.label: the commit's contents are loose in the working tree
verify.hint: git reset HEAD^ during the edit pause

steps.title: Commit the first piece
steps.why: Stage one file, commit it with a message about that one thing. The discipline is simply: one concern, one commit, and now you have the chance to apply it retroactively.

steps.title: And the other two
steps.why: Same again, twice. Three commits now exist where one did, each independently reviewable, revertible and cherry-pickable.

steps.title: Resume the rebase
steps.why: `--continue` replays the remaining commits on top of your new ones. Because the tree content is identical to what it was, nothing conflicts.
steps.expect: Five commits on the branch, and HEAD reattached to feature/overhaul.

verify.label: one commit became three, and the other two replayed

steps.title: Prove the content is unchanged
steps.why: The whole point of a history rewrite is that the end state is identical — only the path there is clearer. Diffing against the backup branch proves it. Note that ORIG_HEAD is no use here: the `reset` you ran mid-rebase overwrote it, which is exactly why the backup branch was worth making.
steps.expect: An empty diff: same tree, better history.

verify.label: the final tree is byte-for-byte what it was before the split
the branch now has five commits instead of three
verify.hint: mark the fat commit edit, reset HEAD^, commit the pieces, then --continue

verify.label: each module got its own commit
the first split commit touches exactly one file
verify.hint: stage one file at a time before committing

verify.label: the resulting tree is identical to before the rewrite
verify.hint: branch the tip before rewriting, then diff against it

verify.label: no rebase in progress, clean tree

pitfalls: `git reset HEAD^` during a rebase is `--mixed`: changes stay in the working tree. `--hard` there would destroy the commit you are trying to split.
Commit the pieces before `--continue`. Continuing with uncommitted changes aborts with a complaint, or worse, folds them into the next commit.
For a file that needs splitting internally rather than by file, `git add -p` at this pause is the tool — the same hunk picker, applied retroactively.
Every commit after the split gets a new sha. If the branch is shared, coordinate before force-pushing.
cheatsheet: apply the commit then stop for you
dissolve the commit into working-tree changes
name the tip before any rewrite
prove the tree did not change
